newsitem.title: FRANCE: FEATURE - French Socialist Aubry on parliament's doorstep.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - French Socialist Aubry on parliament's doorstep.

text.p: Martine Aubry, one of France's best known and popular politicians, finds herself these days on unfamiliar ground: asking for votes.
At 46, Aubry has already had a lengthy public career.
But she is for the first time seeking a National Assembly seat in France's May 25-June 1 parliamentary election.

The daughter of former European Commission president Jacques Delors, she is a top strategist to Socialist Party head Lionel Jospin, a former labour minister and a fixture on French television where she debates rival political heavyweights in a dry but forceful manner.

The self-assured mother of one, who also runs a foundation campaigning for youth employment in blighted urban areas, has decided to put down her political roots in a suburban constituency near the fading northern industrial city of Lille.
Like her father, she consistently ranks among the nation's most popular politicians and is virtually always included in lists of likely prime ministers in a Socialist government.
But in her Lille constituency, she is painted by political foes as a Parisian interloper who has parachuted into the area to muscle aside eager locals with her high national profile.

"When I go to Paris, I don't know how to get around. That is how it must be here for her," says Jacques Donnay, 72, her businessman opponent standing for the Gaullist Rally for the Republic, the ruling conservative coalition's senior partner.
TAILOR-MADE CONSTITUENCY
Perhaps her rivals are bitter because she is likely to win.

The odds seem in her favour simply becase of her party affiliation. The outgoing MP, Bernard Davoine, is a Socialist. Jospin won 55 percent of the vote here in the run-off of the 1995 presidential poll which he lost to Gaullist Jacques Chirac.

Aubry is not entirely a stranger in the area, having been elected to the city council on a Socialist slate and working since 1994 as a deputy to Lille's Socialist mayor, former prime minister Pierre Mauroy.
Mauroy helped her along by convincing Bernard Roman, a potential Socialist rival, to step aside so that she could run.

Because of her frequent media appearances, Aubry, a courteous but rarely smiling technocrat in the mould of her father, is far better known in the district than her rivals, according to polls conducted by RPR contender Donnay.

Aubry first stepped into the spotlight when Edith Cresson, France's first woman prime minister, plucked her from the obscurity of state-owned aluminium firm Pechiney to make her labour minister in 1991.
She cast herself as a champion of the jobless and economically hopeless. Her government service ended when the Socialists were ousted in a 1993 centre-right landslide.
As an outsider in her first National Assembly campaign, Aubry is quick to admit that she is surprised by the outpouring of support shown her by area voters.
CHOCOLATES AND CUDDLY TOYS
"They bring us chocolates, they bring cuddly toys, they say nice things to us -- that gives us great pleasure," she told a reporter on the campaign trail.
Though her favourite issues are Europe and jobs, she focuses on local issues when in the Lille suburbs.

"This constituency brings together all of the character of northern France," Aubry said. "It has many assets including a dynamic agricultural sector, large industries and an industrial tradition where workers are very attached to their work."
Donnay faults her for talking a good game but achieving little.

"She talks a lot, but in the end there is little to show for her lovely speeches," he said in a recent interview. "She sees herself as someone who gets out into the field a lot, but her associations never come up with any solutions.
Aubry bristles at the apparent criticism of her foundation, Action against Exclusion (Agir contre l'exclusion), which she launched in 1993 to help find jobs for disadvantaged youths.
"Exclusion" is France's politically correct buzzword for the poor -- those who are so disadvantaged that they are literally excluded from mainstream French life.
"It's pitiful to attack me on that," Aubry said of Donnay's statement. "We must give hope to those young people who are suffering and have lost their faith.
"In any case, what we have been able to accomplish is only a few drops of water in an ocean of exclusion," she adds.

While her father is a symbol of European integration, Aubry toes the Socialist Party's current line in favouring a more cautious approach to European monetary union, going ahead with the plan only if it is found not to harm France's interests.

She argues that the centre-right government's austerity programme, put in place to help France qualify for a single European currency, should not be used as an excuse to ignore record 12.8 percent unemployment.
"The short-term problem in France is to boost consumption, and thus encourage our businesses to invest," she said in a recent television appearance.
